newsitem.title: USA: Mexico sees anti-Cuba fight as costly for US firms.
newsitem.headline: Mexico sees anti-Cuba fight as costly for US firms.

text.p: Recent Mexican legislation will mean a costly fight for U.S. companies that try to sue Mexican firms under U.S. anti-Cuba law, Mexico's foreign minister Jos Angel Gurria said Wednesday.

Under the new Mexican law, Mexican firms could ignore U.S. requests for information that might be used against them, and would be abled to counter sue U.S. companies that pursue damages under the U.S. Helms-Burton Act.
"Basically, it is meant to have a dissuasive power," Gurria said of the Mexican law described as an "antidote" to Helms-Burton.
At the Americas Society here, Gurria said the Mexican legislation would promote negotiation to settle disputes that otherwise would result in costly legal battles.

"You can go tell the company that was probably going to sue: 'Listen, we're going to get in a fight and it is going to be very expensive for you and going to be very expensive for me, so let's not get into a fight, let's talk'," Gurria said.
The controversial U.S. law allows U.S. firms to sue foreign companies that "traffic" in properties confiscated by Cuba after Fidel Castro came to power 37 years ago.
The U.S. State Department said last month that Mexican consortium Grupo Domos was in violation of Helms-Burton, and several company executives would be barred from entering the United States.

The antidote law passed last week would also fine Mexican companies that allow themselves to be sanctioned by U.S. companies under Helms-Burton. In addition, the law stated that Mexican courts will not accept rulings of U.S. courts.
In addition to Mexico, Canada, the European Union and Organization of American States have condemed Helms-Burton as a violation of international law.
"I don't think anybody feels more uncomfortable with Helms-Burton than the U.S. authorities," the foreign minister said.
